fetched_contents.text: Intelligent tutoring system Computer system to provide instruction to learners An intelligent tutoring system (ITS) is a computer system that imitates human tutors and aims to provide immediate and customized instruction or feedback to learners,[1] usually without requiring intervention from a human teacher.[2] ITSs have the common goal of enabling learning in a meaningful and effective manner by using a variety of computing technologies. There are many examples of ITSs being used in both formal education and professional settings in which they have demonstrated their capabilities and limitations. There is a close relationship between intelligent tutoring, cognitive learning theories and design; and there is ongoing research to improve the effectiveness of ITS. An ITS typically aims to replicate the demonstrated benefits of one-to-one, personalized tutoring, in contexts where students would otherwise have access to one-to-many instruction from a single teacher (e.g., classroom lectures), or no teacher at all (e.g., online homework).[3] ITSs are often designed with the goal of providing access to high quality education to each and every student. History Early mechanical systems The possibility of intelligent machines has been discussed for centuries. Blaise Pascal created the first calculating machine capable of mathematical functions in the 17th century simply called Pascal's Calculator. At this time the mathematician and philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz envisioned machines capable of reasoning and applying rules of logic to settle disputes.[4] These early works inspired later developments. The concept of intelligent machines for instructional use date back as early as 1924, when Sidney Pressey of Ohio State University created a mechanical teaching machine to instruct students without a human teacher.[5][6] His machine resembled closely a typewriter with several keys and a window that provided the learner with questions. The Pressey Machine allowed user input and provided immediate feedback by recording their score on a counter.[7] Pressey was influenced by Edward L. Thorndike, a learning theorist and educational psychologist at the Columbia University Teachers' College of the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Thorndike posited laws for maximizing learning. Thorndike's laws included the law of effect, the law of exercise, and the law of recency. By later standards, Pressey's teaching and testing machine would not be considered intelligent as it was mechanically run and was based on one question and answer at a time,[7] but it set an early precedent for future projects. By the 1950s and 1960s, new perspectives on learning were emerging. Burrhus Frederic "B.F." Skinner at Harvard University did not agree with Thorndike's learning theory of connectionism or Pressey's teaching machine. Rather, Skinner was a behaviorist who believed that learners should construct their answers and not rely on recognition.[6] He too, constructed a teaching machine with an incremental mechanical system that would reward students for correct responses to questions.[6] Early electronic systems In the period following the second world war, mechanical binary systems gave way to binary based electronic machines. These machines were considered intelligent when compared to their mechanical counterparts as they had the capacity to make logical decisions. However, the study of defining and recognizing a machine intelligence was still in its infancy. Alan Turing, a mathematician, logician and computer scientist, linked computing systems to thinking. One of his most notable papers outlined a hypothetical test to assess the intelligence of a machine which came to be known as the Turing test. Essentially, the test would have a person communicate with two other agents, a human and a computer asking questions to both recipients. The computer passes the test if it can respond in such a way that the human posing the questions cannot differentiate between the other human and the computer. The Turing test has been used in its essence for more than two decades as a model for current ITS development. The main ideal for ITS systems is to effectively communicate.[7] As early as the 1950s programs were emerging displaying intelligent features. Turing's work as well as later projects by researchers such as Allen Newell, Clifford Shaw, and Herb Simon showed programs capable of creating logical proofs and theorems. Their program, The Logic Theorist exhibited complex symbol manipulation and even generation of new information without direct human control and is considered by some to be the first AI program. Such breakthroughs would inspire the new field of Artificial Intelligence officially named in 1956 by John McCarthy at the Dartmouth Conference.[4] This conference was the first of its kind that was devoted to scientists and research in the field of AI. The latter part of the 1960s and 1970s saw many new CAI (Computer-Assisted instruction) projects that built on advances in computer science. The creation of the ALGOL programming language in 1958 enabled many schools and universities to begin developing Computer Assisted Instruction (CAI) programs. Major computer vendors and federal agencies in the US such as IBM, HP, and the National Science Foundation funded the development of these projects.[8] Early implementations in education focused on programmed instruction (PI), a structure based on a computerized input-output system. Although many supported this form of instruction, there was limited evidence supporting its effectiveness.[7] The programming language LOGO was created in 1967 by Wally Feurzeig, Cynthia Solomon, and Seymour Papert as a language streamlined for education. PLATO, an educational terminal featuring displays, animations, and touch controls that could store and deliver large amounts of course material, was developed by Donald Bitzer in the University of Illinois in the early 1970s. fetched_contents.text: Multi-modal IoT data fusion for real-time sports event analysis and decision support 1. Introduction With the rapid development of Internet of Things (IoT) technology, especially with the continuous advancement of sensor and data acquisition technology, sports event management has ushered in unprecedented changes [1]. From athletes’ physiological data monitoring to real-time perception of event environmental conditions, IoT provides a rich data source for sports events, which makes it possible to optimize event management and decision support. However, with the explosive growth of data volume, how to efficiently process and fuse multimodal data from different sensors has become a difficult problem to be solved [2]. Most of the existing sports event analysis methods focus on a single data source or simplified spatiotemporal modeling [3]. Traditional systems often rely on manual intervention and have problems such as slow response and delayed decision making. Many studies focus on the analysis of sensor data, especially by analyzing athletes’ physiological data (such as heart rate, body temperature, etc.) or environmental data (such as temperature, humidity, etc.) to monitor events, but these methods often ignore spatiotemporal dependencies and cannot simultaneously process multimodal data and capture the dynamic changes of events [4], [5]. For example, CNNs and LSTMs are widely used in image recognition and time series data prediction, but they are usually difficult to effectively fuse the complex relationship between space and time, and have certain limitations in processing multi-source data [6], [7]. Especially when faced with multimodal IoT data, these traditional methods lack sufficient flexibility and adaptability, resulting in the inability to achieve real-time analysis and accurate decision-making [8]. Therefore, existing research has failed to fully address how to perform efficient multimodal data fusion and spatiotemporal feature modeling in complex and dynamic sports event environments. To fill this research gap, this paper proposes the ST-TransBay Model, a real-time sports event analysis and decision support model for multimodal IoT data fusion. The model combines the spatiotemporal graph convolutional network (ST-GCN) and the Transformer deep learning framework, which can fully mine the spatiotemporal features from different sensors (such as athlete physiological data, environmental data, video streams, etc.) and accurately model the dynamic changes in sports events. In addition, this paper introduces the Bayesian optimization method to further optimize the hyperparameters of the model, thereby improving the real-time performance and decision support capabilities of the model. Through the innovative architecture of data fusion and spatiotemporal modeling, the ST-TransBay Model can not only effectively process complex multimodal data, but also provide accurate real-time decision support for sports event management, and has significant theoretical value and application potential. Based on the above innovations, the main contributions of this paper can be summarized into the following four aspects: * Based on the multimodal data generated by the Internet of Things, this paper proposes a deep learning framework that combines the spatiotemporal graph convolutional network (ST-GCN) and Transformer, which can fully mine the spatiotemporal characteristics from different sensors (such as athlete physiological data, environmental data, video streams, etc.), breaking through the limitations of existing methods in data fusion and spatiotemporal modeling, and providing a new technical path for real-time sports event management. * This paper innovatively introduces the Bayesian optimization method into the deep learning framework, optimizes the hyperparameters of the ST-TransBay Model, and improves the stability and accuracy of the model in different data environments while ensuring high efficiency. * This model effectively supports real-time monitoring, prediction and emergency response in events, provides accurate decision-making basis for event organizers and relevant decision makers, provides a new perspective for the field of sports management, and promotes the in-depth application of deep learning technology in sports big data. The following sections are arranged as follows: Section 2 introduces related work, Section 3 elaborates on the methodology, Section 4 presents the experimental design and results, and Section 5 summarizes the paper and discusses future research directions. 2. Related work 2.1. Applications of the Internet of Things (IoT) in sports events The application of the Internet of Things (IoT) technology in sports events has gradually received widespread attention. The review addresses key research questions, including primary AI methods, their effectiveness in improving athletic performance, their potential for injury prediction, sport-specific applications, strategies for translating knowledge, ethical considerations, and remaining research gaps. Following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a comprehensive literature search was conducted across five databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and SPORTDiscus), encompassing studies published between January 2015 and December 2024. After screening 3248 articles, 73 studies met the inclusion criteria (Cohen’s kappa = 0.84). Data were collected on AI techniques, biomechanical parameters, performance metrics, and implementation details. Results revealed a shift from traditional statistical models to advanced machine learning methods. Based on moderate-quality evidence from 12 studies, convolutional neural networks reached 94% agreement with international experts in technique assessment. Computer vision demonstrated accuracy within 15 mm compared to marker-based systems (6 studies, moderate quality). AI-driven training plans showed 25% accuracy improvements (4 studies, limited evidence). Random forest models predicted hamstring injuries with 85% accuracy (3 studies, moderate quality). Learning management systems enhanced knowledge transfer, raising coaches’ understanding by 45% and athlete adherence by 3.4 times. Implementing integrated AI systems resulted in a 23% reduction in reinjury rates. However, significant challenges remain, including standardizing data, improving model interpretability, validating models in real-world settings, and integrating them into coaching routines. In summary, incorporating AI into sports biomechanics marks a groundbreaking advancement, providing analytical capabilities that surpass traditional techniques. Future research should focus on creating explainable AI, applying rigorous validation methods, handling data ethically, and ensuring equitable access to promote the widespread and responsible use of AI across all levels of competitive sports. This field has undergone a significant transformation with the integration of computational methods. Standard methods for biomechanical analysis utilize laboratory-based facilities, followed by data analysis by highly qualified personnel. Both approaches are quite time-consuming and do not fully represent the affordance of flexibility in on-field sport engagement [2]. These limitations have driven the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into sports biomechanics research. AI encompasses machine learning (ML), neural networks (NN), and deep learning (DL) techniques that enable pattern recognition and predictive modeling from complex datasets [3]. Systematic reviews have established taxonomies for AI applications in sports, distinguishing supervised learning (classification/regression), unsupervised learning (pattern discovery), and deep learning architectures for complex biomechanical analysis [3,4]. Deep learning utilizes multi-layered neural networks for complex pattern recognition, while computer vision processes visual data for automated movement analysis [3,5]. The new generation of deep neural networks has enhanced the ability to analyze large datasets and accurately identify precise movement patterns. The increase in computational power, sensor technology, and algorithms has created a need to rethink how movement data are analyzed. AI techniques now enable the extraction of advanced patterns from vast, multivariate datasets that were previously undetectable to human analysts [5,6]. Additionally, learning management systems (LMS) now serve as critical knowledge translation platforms, transforming complex biomechanical insights into actionable formats for coaches and athletes, effectively bridging the gap between laboratory analysis and field application [7]. fetched_contents.text: Privacy, ethics, transparency, and accountability in AI systems for wearable devices Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) into wearable sensor technologies has substantially advanced health data science, enabling continuous monitoring, personalised interventions, and predictive analytics. However, the fast advancement of these technologies has raised critical ethical and regulatory concerns, particularly around data privacy, algorithmic bias, informed consent, and the opacity of automated decision-making. This study undertakes a systematic examination of these challenges, highlighting the risks posed by unregulated data aggregation, biased model training, and inadequate transparency in AI-powered health applications. Through an analysis of current privacy frameworks and empirical assessment of publicly available datasets, the study identifies significant disparities in model performance across demographic groups and exposes vulnerabilities in both technical design and ethical governance. To address these issues, this article introduces a data-driven methodological framework that embeds transparency, accountability, and regulatory alignment across all stages of AI development. The framework operationalises ethical principles through concrete mechanisms, including explainable AI, bias mitigation techniques, and consent-aware data processing pipelines, while aligning with legal standards such as the GDPR, the UK Data Protection Act, and the EU AI Act. By incorporating transparency as a structural and procedural requirement, the framework presented in this article offers a replicable model for the responsible development of AI systems in wearable healthcare. In doing so, the study advocates for a regulatory paradigm that balances technological innovation with the protection of individual rights, fostering fair, secure, and trustworthy AI-driven health monitoring. Introduction The proliferation of devices capable of continuous physiological monitoring, ranging from consumer-grade smartwatches to clinically validated biosensors, has enabled the capture of vast volumes of personal health data at an unprecedented scale and temporal resolution. When analysed through advanced algorithmic techniques, these data streams offer considerable promise in advancing diagnostic accuracy, facilitating personalised interventions, and supporting population-level health insights. Yet the very features that render these systems powerful also give rise to a complex set of ethical, legal, and epistemological challenges. The passive and pervasive nature of data collection, the opacity of model inference, and the risk of algorithmic discrimination all call into question the adequacy of existing regulatory frameworks. In particular, the conflation of technical sophistication with clinical utility has, in some cases, obscured the normative dimensions of automated health decision-making. This is especially pertinent where decisions are derived from models that are neither explainable to end-users nor fully auditable by developers, thereby eroding the conditions necessary for trust, autonomy, and accountability. This raises many ethical issues on data privacy, consent, bias and fairness, security vulnerabilities (1), and poses significant risks if misused or inadequately protected (2). A growing body of scholarship has articulated the need for ethical and regulatory reform in this domain. However, much of the discourse remains either abstractly principled or overly reactive to high-profile failures. What remains underdeveloped is a systematic, implementable framework that aligns the affordances of data-driven methodologies with the imperatives of transparency, fairness, and regulatory compliance, particularly in the context of wearable systems operating in health-sensitive environments. This article seeks to address that gap. It offers a critical examination of the ethical tensions inherent in AI-enabled wearables and introduces a new methodological framework that operationalises core principles of responsible AI. By embedding transparency and accountability throughout the data lifecycle, from collection and preprocessing to modelling and deployment, the framework provides a normative and technical structure for aligning innovation with public values. In doing so, this study contributes to the field of health informatics but also to the broader discourse on the governance of emerging technologies in data-rich societies. 2. System architecture and design principles for a sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system should be understood as a layered pipeline that integrates user input, sensor data, coaching logic, and real-time feedback. The foundational definition of an intelligent tutoring system (ITS) is a computer system that imitates human tutors and aims to provide immediate and customized instruction or feedback to learners, usually without requiring intervention from a human teacher [N1-R1]. This aligns with the broader educational technology framing that ITSs are computer-based training programs using artificial intelligence to tailor multimedia learning by providing immediate feedback and targeted instruction [N1-R4]. The design goal is therefore not just to collect data but to process and act on it in ways that replicate the benefits of one-on-one tutoring, especially in contexts where students otherwise have access to one-to-many instruction or no teacher at all [N1-R1].

The architecture must integrate user input, sensor data, and coaching logic through a clear flow of data collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, and decision-making. User input can come from the learner’s actions during practice, such as movement, posture, or real-time responses to feedback, while sensor data is captured from wearable devices, motion capture systems, GPS, heart rate monitors, and environmental sensors [N3-F3]. The ST-TransBay model example shows that multimodal sports data fusion can combine physiological data, environmental data, and video streams, while also emphasizing the need to mine spatiotemporal features and handle dynamic changes in events [N2-F2]. This suggests that the system should not treat each data stream separately but should fuse them in a way that preserves their spatiotemporal relationships, which is a key design principle for sports tutoring systems [N2-F2].

Data preprocessing, feature extraction, and decision-making components each have distinct roles. Preprocessing is necessary because multimodal data from different sensors may arrive at different rates, have different formats, and contain noise or missing values. The ST-TransBay paper explicitly identifies the challenge of how to efficiently process and fuse multimodal data from different sensors, noting that existing methods often rely on manual intervention and have problems with slow response and delayed decision making [N2-F2]. Feature extraction then transforms raw sensor readings into meaningful representations for downstream analysis. In sports biomechanics, AI methods use multimodal stacks of various data streams together from wearable sensors, computer motion capture systems, or other sources [N3-R2]. This means feature extraction should combine both numeric sensor data and visual/motion data, as well as contextual environmental data where relevant [N3-R2]. Decision-making components, including coaching logic, must then interpret these features and generate actionable recommendations, feedback, or training plans. The ITS literature emphasizes immediate and customized instruction or feedback [N1-R1], while sports tutoring examples include personalized training, injury prediction, and data-driven insights [N8-R1]. Together, these components form a pipeline that moves from raw data to actionable tutoring output.

The system can scale from single-user tutoring to broader coaching applications by modularizing the architecture and using a shared core that supports multiple users or sessions. ITS literature describes systems designed for student-athletes to enhance academic engagement and motivation, indicating that the same technical architecture can be adapted to sports learning and training [N1-R3]. The multimodal fusion literature similarly shows that real-time sports event analysis and decision support can be built on multi-modal IoT data, which implies that the same fusion and inference infrastructure can be reused across multiple athletes or events [N2-R1]. For deployment, the system should support both individualized tutoring and group coaching by separating the core analysis engine from the user-facing interface and feedback delivery mechanism. The real-time feedback loop is therefore not an afterthought but a central design element that enables the system to respond dynamically as the learner performs, rather than only after the session ends [N2-F2].

Real-time feedback loops fit into the overall architecture through a tightly coupled pipeline that includes sensing, processing, fusion, and immediate action. The ST-TransBay model is explicitly described as a real-time model for multimodal IoT data fusion, combining spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks and a Transformer framework [N2-F2]. This architecture is optimized for real-time performance and decision support, and it is complemented by Bayesian optimization to improve hyperparameter stability and accuracy [N2-F2]. In practice, real-time feedback can be enabled by pipeline stages that handle data alignment, synchronization, and noise handling before the fusion and decision-making components act on the data. The evidence also highlights that multimodal systems leverage the strengths of each modality to compensate for the weaknesses of others [N2-R2], which implies that the architecture should include mechanisms for temporal alignment and noise filtering so that delays or artifacts in one modality do not degrade the overall tutoring experience [N2-R2]. The real-time feedback loop therefore operates as a closed loop: the learner performs, sensors capture data, the system preprocesses and fuses the data, the model produces coaching output, and the system delivers feedback immediately, allowing the learner to adjust and repeat in a continuous cycle [N2-F2].

Multimodal fusion methods and technical implementation for a sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system should be grounded in the complementary strengths of different data modalities. The evidence shows that multimodal systems combine video, audio, and motion data from teaching sessions [N2-R3], while sports event analysis and decision support systems combine physiological data, environmental data, and video streams [N2-F2]. These modalities are complementary because each captures a different aspect of the learning or coaching environment: motion data reflects movement patterns, physiological data reflects the athlete’s internal state, environmental data reflects conditions affecting performance, and visual/audio data can provide contextual cues or instructor behavior [N2-F2]. The multimodal fusion literature also explicitly states that multimodal systems offer the advantage of leveraging the strengths of each modality to compensate for the weaknesses of others [N2-R2], which is especially important in sports settings where no single sensor or modality can fully capture the complexity of performance and feedback needs [N2-R2].

Data alignment, synchronization, and noise handling are critical challenges that must be addressed in the fusion pipeline. The ST-TransBay paper notes that existing sports event analysis methods often focus on a single data source or simplified spatiotemporal modeling, and that traditional methods often ignore spatiotemporal dependencies and cannot simultaneously process multimodal data and capture dynamic changes [N2-F2]. It also states that CNNs and LSTMs are widely used in image recognition and time series data prediction but are difficult to effectively fuse complex relationships between space and time and have limitations in processing multi-source data [N2-F2]. This directly supports the conclusion that the system must explicitly handle synchronization across asynchronous data streams and that simple late or early fusion may not be sufficient. The evidence also indicates that multimodal IoT data fusion is necessary because the data volume is explosive, and the goal is to process and fuse multimodal data from different sensors in real time [N2-F2]. Therefore, the fusion pipeline should include mechanisms for temporal alignment, missing data handling, and noise reduction before the data enter the fusion stage.

The best-suited machine learning models or architectures depend on the task, but the evidence points to deep learning and hybrid architectures as the most promising. The ST-TransBay model combines a spatiotemporal graph convolutional network (ST-GCN) and a Transformer deep learning framework [N2-F2]. This architecture is especially appropriate for sports tutoring and coaching because it can mine spatiotemporal features from different sensors and accurately model dynamic changes [N2-F2]. The same evidence also highlights the need for Bayesian optimization to improve hyperparameters and real-time performance [N2-F2]. In sports biomechanics, AI methods use multimodal stacks of data streams and deep learning techniques such as CNNs, computer vision, and random forest models, with some studies showing high accuracy in movement assessment and injury prediction [N3-F3]. This suggests that the system should consider a family of models, including CNNs for visual data, recurrent models for time-dependent physiological data, and Transformers or GNNs for spatiotemporal data, rather than relying on a single fixed architecture [N2-F2][N3-F3].

Real-time feedback is enabled by the fusion pipeline through efficient processing and low-latency inference. The ST-TransBay paper emphasizes that its model is designed for real-time sports event analysis and decision support and uses Bayesian optimization to improve real-time performance and decision support capabilities [N2-F2]. The multimodal fusion literature also states that real-time decision support is a key application of multi-modal IoT data fusion [N2-R1]. In sports tutoring, this means the pipeline must be optimized so that data from wearable sensors, motion capture, video, and environmental sensors can be processed and fused quickly enough to generate actionable feedback before the athlete finishes the movement or session. The evidence also supports the idea that real-time feedback can be enhanced by integrating computer vision, pose analysis, and voice coaching [N8-R2]. The practical study of AI-based real-time feedback further shows that an AI-driven feedback system can enhance motor skill acquisition [N8-R4]. Together, these sources indicate that the fusion pipeline should be designed with latency, robustness, and modularity in mind, so that feedback can be delivered continuously and responsively during training rather than only after the session ends [N2-F2][N8-R4].

Evaluation and validation strategy for a sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system should be multi-dimensional, covering tutoring quality, user engagement, performance improvement, benchmarks, baselines, user studies, expert validation, field testing, and real-time interaction quality. The evidence suggests that appropriate metrics should be selected based on the system’s goals: immediate and customized instruction or feedback, targeted instruction, and performance improvement [N1-R1][N1-R4]. In sports performance and teaching evaluation, the evidence cites KPIs such as student participation, information retention, instructor efficiency, and athlete adherence [N5-R3]. In sports analytics, the evidence also points to performance metrics such as speed, endurance, and other athlete performance indicators [N3-R4]. For tutoring quality, relevant metrics could include correctness of feedback, relevance of instruction, and alignment with expert coaching principles [N1-R1][N1-R4]. For user engagement, metrics such as session frequency, session duration, and learner interaction with the system can be useful [N5-R3]. For performance improvement, metrics such as skill acquisition, accuracy improvements, and reduced injury risk can be measured [N3-F3][N8-R4].

# Integrated Report on the Construction and Application of a Sports Intelligent Tutoring and Learning Guidance System Driven by Multimodal Data Fusion

## 1. Core Concept and System Purpose

A sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system is best understood as an intelligent tutoring system (ITS) that uses artificial intelligence to provide immediate, customized instruction or feedback to learners, usually without requiring intervention from a human teacher [N1-R1]. The ITS literature frames these systems as computer-based training programs that tailor multimedia learning by providing immediate feedback and targeted instruction [N1-R4]. For sports, this concept extends naturally to coaching and training, where the system aims to support learners in mastering movement skills, improving performance, and receiving personalized guidance rather than relying only on one-to-many instruction or no teacher at all [N1-R1].

The system’s construction is therefore not simply a matter of building a tutoring interface; it is a layered pipeline that integrates user input, sensor data, and coaching logic into a decision-making architecture [N9]. This means the system must collect, preprocess, and fuse multimodal data from the learner’s environment, extract meaningful features, and generate actionable feedback or coaching recommendations [N9]. The evidence also emphasizes that the architecture should support both single-user tutoring and broader coaching applications, making it scalable from individual training sessions to larger coaching workflows [N9].

## 2. System Architecture and Design Principles

### 2.1 Integration of User Input, Sensor Data, and Coaching Logic

The architecture should be viewed as a pipeline in which the learner’s actions and performance generate user input, while wearable and environmental sensors capture physiological, kinematic, and contextual data [N3-F3]. The system then processes these inputs through preprocessing, feature extraction, and decision-making components before delivering feedback or coaching recommendations [N9].

User input can include real-time responses to feedback, movement patterns, posture, and other interactive behaviors, while sensor data come from wearable devices, motion capture, GPS, heart rate monitors, and environmental sensors [N3-F3]. The ST-TransBay model example shows that multimodal sports data fusion can combine physiological data, environmental data, and video streams, and that this fusion is necessary because existing methods often focus on single data sources or simplified spatiotemporal modeling [N2-F2]. In other words, the system should not treat each data stream separately but should integrate them in a way that preserves their spatiotemporal relationships [N2-F2].

### 2.2 Roles of Data Preprocessing, Feature Extraction, and Decision-Making Components

- **Data preprocessing** is essential because multimodal data from different sensors may arrive at different rates, have different formats, and contain noise or missing values [N9]. The ST-TransBay paper explicitly identifies the challenge of how to efficiently process and fuse multimodal data from different sensors, noting that existing methods often rely on manual intervention and have problems with slow response and delayed decision making [N2-F2].
- **Feature extraction** transforms raw sensor readings into meaningful representations for downstream analysis. In sports biomechanics, AI methods use multimodal stacks of various data streams together from wearable sensors, computer motion capture systems, or other sources [N3-R2]. This means feature extraction should combine numeric sensor data, visual/motion data, and contextual environmental data where relevant [N3-R2].
- **Decision-making components** then interpret these features and generate actionable recommendations, feedback, or training plans. The ITS literature emphasizes immediate and customized instruction or feedback [N1-R1], while sports tutoring examples include personalized training, injury prediction, and data-driven insights [N8-R1]. Together, these components form a pipeline that moves from raw data to actionable tutoring output [N9].

### 2.3 Scaling from Single-User Tutoring to Broader Coaching Applications

The system can scale from single-user tutoring to broader coaching applications by modularizing the architecture and using a shared core that supports multiple users or sessions [N9]. ITS literature describes systems designed for student-athletes to enhance academic engagement and motivation, indicating that the same technical architecture can be adapted to sports learning and training [N1-R3]. The multimodal fusion literature similarly shows that real-time sports event analysis and decision support can be built on multi-modal IoT data, which implies that the same fusion and inference infrastructure can be reused across multiple athletes or events [N2-R1].

For deployment, the system should separate the core analysis engine from the user-facing interface and feedback delivery mechanism. This allows the core to remain consistent across users, while the interface can be adapted for different coaching contexts [N9]. The real-time feedback loop is therefore not an afterthought but a central design element that enables the system to respond dynamically as the learner performs, rather than only after the session ends [N9].

### 2.4 Real-Time Feedback Loops in the Architecture

Real-time feedback loops fit into the overall architecture through a tightly coupled pipeline that includes sensing, processing, fusion, and immediate action [N9]. The ST-TransBay model is explicitly described as a real-time model for multimodal IoT data fusion, combining spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks and a Transformer framework [N2-F2]. This architecture is optimized for real-time performance and decision support, and it is complemented by Bayesian optimization to improve hyperparameter stability and accuracy [N2-F2].

In practice, real-time feedback can be enabled by pipeline stages that handle data alignment, synchronization, and noise handling before the fusion and decision-making components act on the data [N9]. The evidence also highlights that multimodal systems leverage the strengths of each modality to compensate for the weaknesses of others [N2-R2], which implies that the architecture should include mechanisms for temporal alignment and noise filtering so that delays or artifacts in one modality do not degrade the overall tutoring experience [N2-R2]. The real-time feedback loop therefore operates as a closed loop: the learner performs, sensors capture data, the system preprocesses and fuses the data, the model produces coaching output, and the system delivers feedback immediately, allowing the learner to adjust and repeat in a continuous cycle [N9].

## 3. Multimodal Fusion Methods and Technical Implementation

### 3.1 Which Modalities Are Fused and Why They Are Complementary

The multimodal fusion evidence shows that the most common modalities in sports tutoring are video, audio, motion data, physiological data, environmental data, and sometimes text or contextual data [N2-R3][N2-F2]. These modalities are complementary because each captures a different aspect of the learning or coaching environment:

- **Motion data** reflect movement patterns and posture [N2-R3].
- **Physiological data** reflect the athlete’s internal state, such as heart rate, temperature, and fatigue [N2-F2].
- **Environmental data** reflect conditions affecting performance, such as temperature, humidity, and lighting [N2-F2].
- **Video/audio data** provide contextual cues, instructor behavior, or real-time feedback [N2-R3].
- **Sensor data** capture kinematic, GPS, and wearable physiological signals [N3-F3].

The multimodal fusion literature explicitly states that multimodal systems offer the advantage of leveraging the strengths of each modality to compensate for the weaknesses of others [N2-R2]. This is especially important in sports settings where no single sensor or modality can fully capture the complexity of performance and feedback needs [N2-R2].

### 3.2 How Data Alignment, Synchronization, and Noise Handling Are Addressed

Data alignment, synchronization, and noise handling are critical challenges that must be addressed in the fusion pipeline. The ST-TransBay paper notes that existing sports event analysis methods often focus on a single data source or simplified spatiotemporal modeling, and that traditional methods often ignore spatiotemporal dependencies and cannot simultaneously process multimodal data and capture dynamic changes [N2-F2]. It also states that CNNs and LSTMs are widely used in image recognition and time series data prediction but are difficult to effectively fuse complex relationships between space and time and have limitations in processing multi-source data [N2-F2].

This directly supports the conclusion that the system must explicitly handle synchronization across asynchronous data streams and that simple late or early fusion may not be sufficient. The evidence also indicates that multimodal IoT data fusion is necessary because the data volume is explosive, and the goal is to process and fuse multimodal data from different sensors in real time [N2-F2]. Therefore, the fusion pipeline should include mechanisms for temporal alignment, missing data handling, and noise reduction before the data enter the fusion stage [N2-F2].

System architecture and design principles for a sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system should be understood as a layered pipeline that integrates user input, sensor data, coaching logic, and real-time feedback. The foundational definition of an intelligent tutoring system (ITS) is a computer system that imitates human tutors and aims to provide immediate and customized instruction or feedback to learners, usually without requiring intervention from a human teacher [N1-R1]. This aligns with the broader educational technology framing that ITSs are computer-based training programs using artificial intelligence to tailor multimedia learning by providing immediate feedback and targeted instruction [N1-R4]. The design goal is therefore not just to collect data but to process and act on it in ways that replicate the benefits of one-on-one tutoring, especially in contexts where students otherwise have access to one-to-many instruction or no teacher at all [N1-R1].

The architecture must integrate user input, sensor data, and coaching logic through a clear flow of data collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, and decision-making. User input can come from the learner’s actions during practice, such as movement, posture, or real-time responses to feedback, while sensor data is captured from wearable devices, motion capture systems, GPS, heart rate monitors, and environmental sensors [N3-F3]. The ST-TransBay model example shows that multimodal sports data fusion can combine physiological data, environmental data, and video streams, while also emphasizing the need to mine spatiotemporal features and handle dynamic changes in events [N2-F2]. This suggests that the system should not treat each data stream separately but should fuse them in a way that preserves their spatiotemporal relationships, which is a key design principle for sports tutoring systems [N2-F2].

Data preprocessing, feature extraction, and decision-making components each have distinct roles. Preprocessing is necessary because multimodal data from different sensors may arrive at different rates, have different formats, and contain noise or missing values. The ST-TransBay paper explicitly identifies the challenge of how to efficiently process and fuse multimodal data from different sensors, noting that existing methods often rely on manual intervention and have problems with slow response and delayed decision making [N2-F2]. Feature extraction then transforms raw sensor readings into meaningful representations for downstream analysis. In sports biomechanics, AI methods use multimodal stacks of various data streams together from wearable sensors, computer motion capture systems, or other sources [N3-R2]. This means feature extraction should combine both numeric sensor data and visual/motion data, as well as contextual environmental data where relevant [N3-R2]. Decision-making components, including coaching logic, must then interpret these features and generate actionable recommendations, feedback, or training plans. The ITS literature emphasizes immediate and customized instruction or feedback [N1-R1], while sports tutoring examples include personalized training, injury prediction, and data-driven insights [N8-R1]. Together, these components form a pipeline that moves from raw data to actionable tutoring output.

The system can scale from single-user tutoring to broader coaching applications by modularizing the architecture and using a shared core that supports multiple users or sessions. ITS literature describes systems designed for student-athletes to enhance academic engagement and motivation, indicating that the same technical architecture can be adapted to sports learning and training [N1-R3]. The multimodal fusion literature similarly shows that real-time sports event analysis and decision support can be built on multi-modal IoT data, which implies that the same fusion and inference infrastructure can be reused across multiple athletes or events [N2-R1]. For deployment, the system should support both individualized tutoring and group coaching by separating the core analysis engine from the user-facing interface and feedback delivery mechanism. The real-time feedback loop is therefore not an afterthought but a central design element that enables the system to respond dynamically as the learner performs, rather than only after the session ends [N2-F2].

Real-time feedback loops fit into the overall architecture through a tightly coupled pipeline that includes sensing, processing, fusion, and immediate action. The ST-TransBay model is explicitly described as a real-time model for multimodal IoT data fusion, combining spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks and a Transformer framework [N2-F2]. This architecture is optimized for real-time performance and decision support, and it is complemented by Bayesian optimization to improve hyperparameter stability and accuracy [N2-F2]. In practice, real-time feedback can be enabled by pipeline stages that handle data alignment, synchronization, and noise handling before the fusion and decision-making components act on the data. The evidence also highlights that multimodal systems leverage the strengths of each modality to compensate for the weaknesses of others [N2-R2], which implies that the architecture should include mechanisms for temporal alignment and noise filtering so that delays or artifacts in one modality do not degrade the overall tutoring experience [N2-R2]. The real-time feedback loop therefore operates as a closed loop: the learner performs, sensors capture data, the system preprocesses and fuses the data, the model produces coaching output, and the system delivers feedback immediately, allowing the learner to adjust and repeat in a continuous cycle [N2-F2].

Multimodal fusion methods and technical implementation for a sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system should be grounded in the complementary strengths of different data modalities. The evidence shows that multimodal systems combine video, audio, and motion data from teaching sessions [N2-R3], while sports event analysis and decision support systems combine physiological data, environmental data, and video streams [N2-F2]. These modalities are complementary because each captures a different aspect of the learning or coaching environment: motion data reflects movement patterns, physiological data reflects the athlete’s internal state, environmental data reflects conditions affecting performance, and visual/audio data can provide contextual cues or instructor behavior [N2-F2]. The multimodal fusion literature also explicitly states that multimodal systems offer the advantage of leveraging the strengths of each modality to compensate for the weaknesses of others [N2-R2], which is especially important in sports settings where no single sensor or modality can fully capture the complexity of performance and feedback needs [N2-R2].

Data alignment, synchronization, and noise handling are critical challenges that must be addressed in the fusion pipeline. The ST-TransBay paper notes that existing sports event analysis methods often focus on a single data source or simplified spatiotemporal modeling, and that traditional methods often ignore spatiotemporal dependencies and cannot simultaneously process multimodal data and capture dynamic changes [N2-F2]. It also states that CNNs and LSTMs are widely used in image recognition and time series data prediction but are difficult to effectively fuse complex relationships between space and time and have limitations in processing multi-source data [N2-F2]. This directly supports the conclusion that the system must explicitly handle synchronization across asynchronous data streams and that simple late or early fusion may not be sufficient. The evidence also indicates that multimodal IoT data fusion is necessary because the data volume is explosive, and the goal is to process and fuse multimodal data from different sensors in real time [N2-F2]. Therefore, the fusion pipeline should include mechanisms for temporal alignment, missing data handling, and noise reduction before the data enter the fusion stage.

The best-suited machine learning models or architectures depend on the task, but the evidence points to deep learning and hybrid architectures as the most promising. The ST-TransBay model combines a spatiotemporal graph convolutional network (ST-GCN) and a Transformer deep learning framework [N2-F2]. This architecture is especially appropriate for sports tutoring and coaching because it can mine spatiotemporal features from different sensors and accurately model dynamic changes [N2-F2]. The same evidence also highlights the need for Bayesian optimization to improve hyperparameters and real-time performance [N2-F2]. In sports biomechanics, AI methods use multimodal stacks of data streams and deep learning techniques such as CNNs, computer vision, and random forest models, with some studies showing high accuracy in movement assessment and injury prediction [N3-F3]. This suggests that the system should consider a family of models, including CNNs for visual data, recurrent models for time-dependent physiological data, and Transformers or GNNs for spatiotemporal data, rather than relying on a single fixed architecture [N2-F2][N3-F3].

Real-time feedback is enabled by the fusion pipeline through efficient processing and low-latency inference. The ST-TransBay paper emphasizes that its model is designed for real-time sports event analysis and decision support and uses Bayesian optimization to improve real-time performance and decision support capabilities [N2-F2]. In sports performance and teaching evaluation, the evidence cites KPIs such as student participation, information retention, instructor efficiency, and athlete adherence [N5-R3]. In sports analytics, the evidence also points to performance metrics such as speed, endurance, and other athlete performance indicators [N3-R4]. For tutoring quality, relevant metrics could include correctness of feedback, relevance of instruction, and alignment with expert coaching principles [N1-R1][N1-R4]. For user engagement, metrics such as session frequency, session duration, and learner interaction with the system can be useful [N5-R3]. For performance improvement, metrics such as skill acquisition, accuracy improvements, and reduced injury risk can be measured [N3-F3][N8-R4].

Benchmarks and baselines should be established by comparing the system against both human coaching and existing tutoring approaches. The ITS literature indicates that ITSs are often compared to one-to-many instruction from a single teacher or no teacher at all [N1-R1]. Benchmarks should be quantitative, such as accuracy improvements, reduction in reinjury rates, or improvement in technique assessment [N3-F3]. Baselines should include simple rule-based systems or traditional coaching methods so that the AI-driven system’s gains can be meaningfully assessed [N1-R1][N8-R2]. The evidence also supports the use of comparative studies in sports coaching, which can include real training data and case studies [N6-R3]. User studies, expert validation, and field testing should be designed to capture both technical performance and human experience. The most suitable sports domains and learner populations appear to be elite sports, youth sports, physical education, and rehabilitation settings. Major limitations and failure modes include data quality issues, model bias, and failure to generalize across contexts. The evidence states that wearable sensors present challenges in correctly collecting data [N7-R1], implying that poor sensor placement, interference, or inconsistent sampling can degrade system performance. The privacy and ethics literature warns that biases in training algorithms may create unfair advantages or disadvantages, while privacy breaches could expose sensitive athlete data [N7-R2]. The same source also notes that AI and ML algorithms can inadvertently perpetuate or exaggerate societal biases, especially when trained on data from wearables that may underrepresent certain demographics [N7-F4]. In sports tutoring, this means the system could produce inaccurate or unfair feedback if the training data are not representative of the target population [N7-R2][N7-F4]. Another failure mode is the inability of the system to handle dynamic, unstructured, or rare events, which the multimodal fusion literature notes by emphasizing that traditional methods often ignore spatiotemporal dependencies and cannot simultaneously process multimodal data and capture dynamic changes [N2-F2]. The evidence also highlights the need for real-time performance and decision support, which introduces additional reliability and latency constraints [N2-F2].

Privacy, ethics, and practical deployment barriers are substantial. The privacy and ethics literature explicitly states that wearable sensors raise ethical and regulatory concerns around data privacy, informed consent, algorithmic bias, and the opacity of automated decision-making [N7-F4]. It also identifies significant disparities in model performance across demographic groups and vulnerabilities in both technical design and ethical governance [N7-F4]. The evidence further notes that unauthorized access or misuse of wearable data has led to severe ethical privacy concerns, and that processing athletes’ data through wearable technology can involve privacy, confidentiality, ownership, use, and sharing issues [N7-R3][N7-R4]. College athletes’ data privacy concerns are also highlighted, including the lack of regulation by the NCAA and the lack of protection under HIPAA [N7-R5]. These barriers suggest that deployment requires careful attention to consent, data security, and regulatory compliance [N7-R1][N7-R4][N7-R5].

In sports, this is especially valuable because coaching is iterative: athletes need repeated feedback, adjustments, and reinforcement over time. The use of real-time feedback, pose analysis, voice coaching, and computer vision in AI coaching systems further supports continuous learning, because the system can adapt in response to each performance cycle [N8-R2][N8-R4]. In contrast, one-time assessment is less central to the architecture, since the evidence emphasizes real-time decision support, prediction, and personalized training [N2-F2][N8-R1]. # Integrated Report on the Construction and Application of a Sports Intelligent Tutoring and Learning Guidance System Driven by Multimodal Data Fusion

## 1. Core Concept and System Purpose

A sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system is best understood as an intelligent tutoring system (ITS) that uses artificial intelligence to provide immediate, customized instruction or feedback to learners, usually without requiring intervention from a human teacher [N1-R1]. The ITS literature frames these systems as computer-based training programs that tailor multimedia learning by providing immediate feedback and targeted instruction [N1-R4]. For sports, this concept extends naturally to coaching and training, where the system aims to support learners in mastering movement skills, improving performance, and receiving personalized guidance rather than relying only on one-to-many instruction or no teacher at all [N1-R1].

The system’s construction is therefore not simply a matter of building a tutoring interface; it is a layered pipeline that integrates user input, sensor data, and coaching logic into a decision-making architecture [N9]. This means the system must collect, preprocess, and fuse multimodal data from the learner’s environment, extract meaningful features, and generate actionable feedback or coaching recommendations [N9]. The evidence also emphasizes that the architecture should support both single-user tutoring and broader coaching applications, making it scalable from individual training sessions to larger coaching workflows [N9].

## 2. System Architecture and Design Principles

### 2.1 Integration of User Input, Sensor Data, and Coaching Logic

The architecture should be viewed as a pipeline in which the learner’s actions and performance generate user input, while wearable and environmental sensors capture physiological, kinematic, and contextual data [N3-F3]. The system then processes these inputs through preprocessing, feature extraction, and decision-making components before delivering feedback or coaching recommendations [N9].

User input can include real-time responses to feedback, movement patterns, posture, and other interactive behaviors, while sensor data come from wearable devices, motion capture, GPS, heart rate monitors, and environmental sensors [N3-F3]. The ST-TransBay model example shows that multimodal sports data fusion can combine physiological data, environmental data, and video streams, and that this fusion is necessary because existing methods often focus on single data sources or simplified spatiotemporal modeling [N2-F2]. In other words, the system should not treat each data stream separately but should integrate them in a way that preserves their spatiotemporal relationships [N2-F2].

### 2.2 Roles of Data Preprocessing, Feature Extraction, and Decision-Making Components

- **Data preprocessing** is essential because multimodal data from different sensors may arrive at different rates, have different formats, and contain noise or missing values [N9]. The ST-TransBay paper explicitly identifies the challenge of how to efficiently process and fuse multimodal data from different sensors, noting that existing methods often rely on manual intervention and have problems with slow response and delayed decision making [N2-F2].
- **Feature extraction** transforms raw sensor readings into meaningful representations for downstream analysis. In sports biomechanics, AI methods use multimodal stacks of various data streams together from wearable sensors, computer motion capture systems, or other sources [N3-R2]. This means feature extraction should combine numeric sensor data, visual/motion data, and contextual environmental data where relevant [N3-R2].
- **Decision-making components** then interpret these features and generate actionable recommendations, feedback, or training plans. The ITS literature emphasizes immediate and customized instruction or feedback [N1-R1], while sports tutoring examples include personalized training, injury prediction, and data-driven insights [N8-R1]. Together, these components form a pipeline that moves from raw data to actionable tutoring output [N9].

### 2.3 Scaling from Single-User Tutoring to Broader Coaching Applications

The system can scale from single-user tutoring to broader coaching applications by modularizing the architecture and using a shared core that supports multiple users or sessions [N9]. ITS literature describes systems designed for student-athletes to enhance academic engagement and motivation, indicating that the same technical architecture can be adapted to sports learning and training [N1-R3]. The multimodal fusion literature similarly shows that real-time sports event analysis and decision support can be built on multi-modal IoT data, which implies that the same fusion and inference infrastructure can be reused across multiple athletes or events [N2-R1].

For deployment, the system should separate the core analysis engine from the user-facing interface and feedback delivery mechanism. This allows the core to remain consistent across users, while the interface can be adapted for different coaching contexts [N9]. The real-time feedback loop is therefore not an afterthought but a central design element that enables the system to respond dynamically as the learner performs, rather than only after the session ends [N9].

### 2.4 Real-Time Feedback Loops in the Architecture

Real-time feedback loops fit into the overall architecture through a tightly coupled pipeline that includes sensing, processing, fusion, and immediate action [N9]. The ST-TransBay model is explicitly described as a real-time model for multimodal IoT data fusion, combining spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks and a Transformer framework [N2-F2]. This architecture is optimized for real-time performance and decision support, and it is complemented by Bayesian optimization to improve hyperparameter stability and accuracy [N2-F2].

In practice, real-time feedback can be enabled by pipeline stages that handle data alignment, synchronization, and noise handling before the fusion and decision-making components act on the data [N9]. The evidence also highlights that multimodal systems leverage the strengths of each modality to compensate for the weaknesses of others [N2-R2], which implies that the architecture should include mechanisms for temporal alignment and noise filtering so that delays or artifacts in one modality do not degrade the overall tutoring experience [N2-R2]. The real-time feedback loop therefore operates as a closed loop: the learner performs, sensors capture data, the system preprocesses and fuses the data, the model produces coaching output, and the system delivers feedback immediately, allowing the learner to adjust and repeat in a continuous cycle [N9].

## 3. Multimodal Fusion Methods and Technical Implementation

### 3.1 Which Modalities Are Fused and Why They Are Complementary

The multimodal fusion evidence shows that the most common modalities in sports tutoring are video, audio, motion data, physiological data, environmental data, and sometimes text or contextual data [N2-R3][N2-F2]. These modalities are complementary because each captures a different aspect of the learning or coaching environment:

- **Motion data** reflect movement patterns and posture [N2-R3].
- **Physiological data** reflect the athlete’s internal state, such as heart rate, temperature, and fatigue [N2-F2].
- **Environmental data** reflect conditions affecting performance, such as temperature, humidity, and lighting [N2-F2].
- **Video/audio data** provide contextual cues, instructor behavior, or real-time feedback [N2-R3].
- **Sensor data** capture kinematic, GPS, and wearable physiological signals [N3-F3].

The multimodal fusion literature explicitly states that multimodal systems offer the advantage of leveraging the strengths of each modality to compensate for the weaknesses of others [N2-R2]. This is especially important in sports settings where no single sensor or modality can fully capture the complexity of performance and feedback needs [N2-R2].

### 3.2 How Data Alignment, Synchronization, and Noise Handling Are Addressed

Data alignment, synchronization, and noise handling are critical challenges that must be addressed in the fusion pipeline. The ST-TransBay paper notes that existing sports event analysis methods often focus on a single data source or simplified spatiotemporal modeling, and that traditional methods often ignore spatiotemporal dependencies and cannot simultaneously process multimodal data and capture dynamic changes [N2-F2]. It also states that CNNs and LSTMs are widely used in image recognition and time series data prediction but are difficult to effectively fuse complex relationships between space and time and have limitations in processing multi-source data [N2-F2].

This directly supports the conclusion that the system must explicitly handle synchronization across asynchronous data streams and that simple late or early fusion may not be sufficient. The evidence also indicates that multimodal IoT data fusion is necessary because the data volume is explosive, and the goal is to process and fuse multimodal data from different sensors in real time [N2-F2]. Therefore, the fusion pipeline should include mechanisms for temporal alignment, missing data handling, and noise reduction before the data enter the fusion stage [N2-F2].

The evidence points to deep learning and hybrid architectures as the most promising. This architecture is especially appropriate for sports tutoring and coaching because it can mine spatiotemporal features from different sensors and accurately model dynamic changes [N2-F2]. The same evidence also highlights the need for Bayesian optimization to improve hyperparameters and real-time performance [N2-F2].

In sports biomechanics, AI methods use multimodal stacks of data streams and deep learning techniques such as CNNs, computer vision, and random forest models, with some studies showing high accuracy in movement assessment and injury prediction [N3-F3]. This suggests that the system should consider a family of models, including CNNs for visual data, recurrent models for time-dependent physiological data, and Transformers or GNNs for spatiotemporal data, rather than relying on a single fixed architecture [N2-F2][N3-F3].

Real-time feedback is enabled by the fusion pipeline through efficient processing and low-latency inference. In sports tutoring, this means the pipeline must be optimized so that data from wearable sensors, motion capture, video, and environmental sensors can be processed and fused quickly enough to generate actionable feedback before the athlete finishes the movement or session [N2-F2].
